claim: Adoptive transfer models using TCR transgenic mice have made it possible to study early T cell responses at clonal level.
source: Adoptive transfer models using TCR transgenic mice as donors of antigen-reactive T cells have made it possible to study early T cell responses at clonal level, which is otherwise very strenuous given the extensive variety of polyclonal T cell clones.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The broad variety of polyclonal T cell clones causes low progenitor frequency of any given clone in the pre-immune repertoire.
source: This broad variety causes low progenitor frequency of any given clone in the pre-immune repertoire, rendering the tracking of early responses exceedingly difficult.
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge.

claim: TCR transgenic models allow study of the functional status of antigen-specific T cells and cell-fate decisions to effector cells, Tfh cells, or memory cells.
source: In addition, these models confer a significant advantage to T cell research, as they allow to study the functional status of antigen-specific T cells, but also cell-fate decisions to effector cells, Tfh cells, or memory cells (Grayson et al., 2000; Mueller et al., 2010; Tubo et al., 2013; West et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The standard method for generating TCR Tg mice comprises immunization, isolation of T cells, and examination of T cell reactivity by in vitro restimulation of T cell hybridoma clones.
source: The standard method for generating TCR Tg mice comprises immunization of an animal, isolation of T cells out of lymphoid organs and examination of T cell reactivity by in vitro restimulation of T cell hybridoma clones.
evidence: This describes the standard practice in the field.

claim: TCRs are identified using PCR primers and antibodies from antigen-specific T cell clones, often without knowing the detailed sequence of the Vα- and Vβ-chains.
source: TCRs are then identified crudely using PCR primers and antibodies from the antigen-specific T cell clones, often without knowing the detailed sequence of the Vα- and Vβ-chains (Barnden et al., 1998; Bosteels et al., 2020; Coquet et al., 2015; Nindl et al., 2012; Oxenius et al., 1998; Plantinga et al., 2013; Vanheerswynghels et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The generation of functional TCR Tg mouse models depends on the selection of the antigen epitope and the ability of selected T cell clones to mount antigen-specific responses.
source: The generation of functional TCR Tg mouse models depends on several key steps. A first essential step is the selection of the antigen epitope, which is either done by using peptide libraries (Zhuang et al., 2021) or by computational scanning combined with a cellular activity assay (Erez et al., 2023; Vandersarren et al., 2017; Vanheerswynghels et al., 2018). Second, the selected T cell clones need to be able to mount antigen-specific responses.
evidence: This is based on the authors' knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: TCRs are currently screened by stimulating them with antigen peptide or co-culture with antigen-pulsed BM-DCs and assessing proliferation, CD69 upregulation and IL-2/IFN-γ cytokine production.
source: The only way that currently TCRs are screened for this essential characteristic is by stimulating them with antigen peptide or co-culture with antigen-pulsed BM-DCs, whereafter their proliferation, CD69 upregulation and IL-2/IFN-γ cytokine production is assessed (Bosteels et al., 2020; Coquet et al., 2015; Nindl et al., 2012; Oxenius et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Current TCR screening assays do not inform on fitness/competition of the clone in a polyclonal environment.
source: While these assays report on the potential to activate the TCR bearing clone, it does not inform on fitness/competition of the ensuing clone in a polyclonal environment, nor is it known what the effect of the TCR will be on Tg T cell development into the cell-fate of interest.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of current methods.

claim: Current TCR screening assays do not inform on the effect of the TCR on Tg T cell development into the cell-fate of interest.
source: While these assays report on the potential to activate the TCR bearing clone, it does not inform on fitness/competition of the ensuing clone in a polyclonal environment, nor is it known what the effect of the TCR will be on Tg T cell development into the cell-fate of interest.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of current methods.

claim: Effector cells are mainly found amongst high-affinity clones.
source: In fact, whereas effector cells are mainly found amongst high-affinity clones, memory cells recognize antigens with lower affinity and benefit from more clonal diversity (Kavazović et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Memory cells recognize antigens with lower affinity and benefit from more clonal diversity.
source: In fact, whereas effector cells are mainly found amongst high-affinity clones, memory cells recognize antigens with lower affinity and benefit from more clonal diversity (Kavazović et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Distinct mechanisms drive effector/memory development in high- and low-affinity T cells, such as regulation of IL-12R signalling, T-bet, and Eomes expression.
source: Distinct mechanisms drive effector/memory development in high- and low-affinity T cells, such as regulation of IL-12R signalling, T-bet, and Eomes expression (Knudson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Upon weak TCR–ligand interactions, expansion of activated naive T cells will stop sooner than after strong TCR–ligand interactions.
source: It has also been shown that upon weak TCR–ligand interactions, expansion of activated naive T cells will stop sooner than after strong TCR–ligand interactions (Zehn et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The strength of tonic signalling determines whether CD4 TCR-transgenic cells will become Tfh cells or not.
source: For instance, using CD4 TCR-transgenic mice, it has been shown that the strength of tonic signalling determines whether the cells will become Tfh cells or not (Bartleson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The potential to react to tonic MHC signals can influence whether a TCR will induce an immediate effector proliferative response or a memory response.
source: The same authors showed that the potential to react to tonic MHC signals, reflected by the potential of a clone to upregulate CD5, can also profoundly influence whether a given TCR will induce and immediate effector proliferative response, or rather give a memory response, even when the affinity of two clones for the same immunodominant epitope is nearly identical (Milam et al., 2018; Weber et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The affinity bias of the TCR–MHC interaction leading to long-term memory and residence, particularly in tissues, is not clear.

evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a gap in current knowledge.

evidence: This is a prediction/speculation by the authors.
